opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where the law is going to have to catch up quickly, because the traditional framework doesn't map neatly onto what these systems do. Defamation law, especially in the U.S. for public figures, leans heavily on intent: did you know it was false, or did you act with reckless disregard for the truth? A large language model doesn't *know* anything in the ordinary sense. It's not lying in the way a person lies. It's doing autocomplete at scale, stitching together statistically plausible fragments, and sometimes that produces a sentence like "Professor So-and-so was accused of harassment," complete with a fabricated citation, when nothing of the sort ever happened.

But I don't think "the machine didn't mean it" should be a get-out-of-jail-free card. The people who build and deploy these systems know, with complete certainty, that they hallucinate. That isn't a secret; it's a well-documented property of the technology. So if you put a product into the world that you know will sometimes generate damaging falsehoods about real, named people, and you market it as a source of information, that starts to look a lot like reckless disregard, just located at the level of the company rather than the individual output.

So my view is that liability should attach to the developers and deployers, not to some imaginary intent in the model. We have analogies for this in product liability. If you sell a car with brakes you know fail some percentage of the time, you don't get to say, "Well, the brakes didn't intend to fail." The question becomes: what did you know, what safeguards could you reasonably have put in place, and did you put them in place?

That also creates the right incentives. Right now the economic incentive is to ship fast and let the public absorb the harms. If companies had to bear some cost when their systems falsely accuse someone of a crime, they'd invest a lot more in things like grounding outputs in verifiable sources, refusing to make factual claims about private individuals, and building real correction mechanisms, so that when someone says, "This is false and it's destroying my reputation," something actually happens.

And I'd add one more thing. I'm very skeptical of the idea that Section 230-style immunity should extend to generative AI. Section 230 was designed for platforms hosting *other people's* speech. When a chatbot generates a defamatory sentence, there's no third-party author. The company's system wrote it. It's hard to see why they should get a shield that was designed for a completely different situation.

None of this is easy, and courts will have to work through hard questions about thresholds and remedies. But the principle should be clear: if you build a machine that predictably manufactures falsehoods about real people, you're responsible for what it says.

r001.rationale: The response treats foreseeable defamatory outputs, given companies’ knowledge of hallucinations and failure to use safeguards, as reckless disregard that can support liability.

r002.rationale: It explicitly rejects “the machine didn’t mean it” as a defense and says responsibility should fall on developers and deployers despite the model not operating like a human.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, the first thing to say is that this isn't hypothetical. These systems have already fabricated accusations about real people. There was the case of a law professor who was falsely described as having been accused of sexual harassment, complete with a citation to a Washington Post article that never existed. There was a radio host in Georgia who sued OpenAI after ChatGPT invented an embezzlement complaint against him. These things happen because the systems don't know anything in the way you and I know things. They're predicting plausible-sounding text, and a plausible-sounding accusation is still an accusation.

Now, the legal problem is that defamation law, at least in the US, was built around human speakers with mental states. For a public figure you have to show actual malice, meaning the speaker knew it was false or recklessly disregarded the truth. A language model doesn't know anything and doesn't disregard anything. So if you take the doctrine literally, you get this absurd result where the more automated the lie, the less anyone is accountable for it. I think that's exactly backwards.

My view is that the mental-state question should attach to the company, not to the machine. OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, whoever, they know perfectly well that these systems hallucinate. It's documented in their own papers. It's in their own terms of service. If you knowingly deploy a product that routinely fabricates facts about real people, and you deploy it to hundreds of millions of users, I think that's a pretty reasonable candidate for recklessness in the legal sense. You don't get to say "we didn't intend it" when you shipped it knowing it does this.

The analogy people reach for is Section 230, the idea that the platform just hosts other people's speech. But that analogy fails completely. The model isn't relaying what someone else said. It generated the sentence. There's no third party. The company is the author in every meaningful sense, and I think courts are going to come around to that.

The other thing I'd say is that this shouldn't just be a liability question, it should be a product-design question. We have mechanisms in other industries. If a car has a defect that injures people, you don't ask whether the car intended it. You ask whether the manufacturer should have known and what they did about it. I'd like to see something similar here, maybe a strict-liability regime for certain categories of harm, like false criminal accusations, where the bar for the plaintiff is simply that the system said it and it wasn't true.

And honestly, part of why I care about this is that liability is one of the few levers that actually changes corporate behavior. If fabricating accusations about real people becomes expensive, suddenly you'll see a lot more investment in retrieval, in verification, in systems that say "I don't know" instead of confabulating. The technology to be more careful largely exists. What's missing is the incentive. Defamation law could supply it.

r001.rationale: The response treats a company’s knowing deployment of systems that fabricate accusations as potentially reckless in the legal sense, grounding liability in what the company knew and should address.

r002.rationale: It calls it absurd that automated lies would face less accountability because the model lacks human mental states, and argues that this should not excuse the company.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish the intentions of the machine from the responsibilities of the people deploying it. The machine doesn’t have malice in the ordinary human sense. But it doesn’t follow that nobody should be accountable when it invents a damaging accusation about a real person.

And “actual malice” is a legal term; it isn’t simply about whether someone wishes you harm. It concerns knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth. How that applies to a company deploying a system is a serious question. Knowing that your system sometimes fabricates things isn’t necessarily the same as knowing that a particular allegation is false. But continuing to circulate that allegation after you’ve been notified seems like a much clearer case for responsibility.

The policy question should be: what reasonable precautions did you take? Did you test for these failures? Can someone get a false accusation corrected? Does the system keep repeating it? A disclaimer that says, essentially, ‘Sometimes we make things up’ shouldn’t automatically absolve you of the consequences.

We need incentives to build systems that are reliable and to respond when they cause harm. We shouldn’t let the absence of a mind inside the machine become an excuse for the absence of accountability outside it.

r001.rationale: The response calls for precautions, correction, and accountability, but does not characterize producing defamatory false accusations as negligence.

r002.rationale: It says the machine’s lack of a mind should not excuse the absence of accountability for harm caused by the people deploying it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to separate the psychology of the machine from the responsibility of the people deploying it. The model doesn’t have malice in the ordinary sense. It doesn’t have beliefs or intentions in the way a person does. But that doesn’t mean somebody who’s falsely accused of a crime hasn’t been harmed.

The legal question should be about what the company knew, what precautions it took, and what it did when it was told about a problem. Actual malice is a technical legal standard, and it isn’t required in every defamation case. We shouldn’t assume that a machine’s lack of intentions resolves the question of its operator’s responsibility.

If you know your system invents things, including accusations about real people, you have an obligation to address that. You can require stronger evidence for damaging claims, have the system abstain when it can’t verify them, and provide a meaningful correction process. A little disclaimer saying ‘this system may make mistakes’ isn’t an adequate answer to someone whose reputation you’ve damaged.

We want useful technology, but we also want accountability. The fact that the words were generated probabilistically shouldn’t leave the person harmed with no recourse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses operator responsibility, precautions, and obligations to address known problems, but it does not characterize the false accusations as negligence.

r002.rationale: It says the model’s lack of human intentions does not resolve operator responsibility and that probabilistic generation should not leave harmed people without recourse, rejecting machine differences as an excuse for serious harm.
